lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- Reporting the Numbers
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Renato Annunciato | Lesson 3 -- Reporting the Numbers

listenings.text: I sit through about forty of these reviews every quarter, and I can tell you exactly what separates a good one from a bad one. It is not the result. A manager can come to me with a terrible number and give me a very good report. What I want is the number first. Not the market, not the weather, not the competitor who did something strange in April. The number, and then the reason. When somebody starts with ten minutes of context, I know what is coming, and so does everybody else on the call. The context becomes an apology. The second thing is the difference between a quarter that is finished and a year that is still open. If you tell me what you did in March, use the past. If you tell me where you are so far this year, that is still moving, and the language has to show it. Managers who mix those two make me ask the same question three times, and after the third time I stop trusting the numbers.

Three years ago I missed my quota by nineteen percent, and I hid it for six weeks. Not deliberately. I kept thinking the pipeline would close and the shortfall would disappear before anybody had to hear about it. It did not. When I finally reported it, the number was the same, but the conversation was completely different from the one I would have had in week one. My director did not care about the nineteen percent. He cared that he had spent six weeks telling his own boss that our region was fine. What I do now is simple. The moment I can see a shortfall coming, I say it, with a date and a plan attached. I say what we have done so far, what we did last month that did not work, and what I am changing. Nobody has ever been punished for reporting a bad number early. People do lose their jobs for reporting it late.

extra_audio.text: Good afternoon. Year to date we have reached ninety-four percent of the target. Growth came from the clinics in the interior, where two consultants outperformed their quota. Last month we missed the forecast in Rio de Janeiro, and that is where the shortfall sits. Next quarter I am moving three large accounts into the new pipeline.
